conflicts/milvian-bridge/name: Constantine at the Milvian Bridge and the Christian empire's wars
conflicts/milvian-bridge/religionRoleNot: These were Roman civil wars for supreme power between rival emperors of the Tetrarchy, and would have been fought whatever the gods of the contenders. Religion entered because Constantine attributed his victory of 312 to the God of the Christians and fought under a Christian sign, and because Christian writers, above all Eusebius of Caesarea, presented his final war against Licinius in 324 as the defeat of a persecutor. Historians have long debated Constantine's sincerity: Jacob Burckhardt saw a calculating politician, while Timothy Barnes and others argue for a real if theologically unsophisticated conversion around 312. Most now accept that he genuinely believed the Christian God gave victory, but that the wars themselves were dynastic and political; religion supplied legitimacy and a new language of divinely sanctioned battle rather than the cause.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/sides/0/name: Constantine (Augustus in the West, from 324 sole emperor)
conflicts/milvian-bridge/sides/0/faith: Favoured Christianity from 312; earlier a devotee of Sol Invictus
conflicts/milvian-bridge/sides/1/faith: Traditional Roman religion; tolerant of Christians in Italy
conflicts/milvian-bridge/sides/2/faith: Traditional Roman religion; co-author of the 313 settlement, later restricted Christians
conflicts/milvian-bridge/summary: Between 312 and 324 Constantine fought his way from Gaul to sole rule of the Roman world, first defeating Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome after, by his own later account, seeing a sign in the sky and being told 'in this sign conquer', and finally overthrowing his eastern colleague Licinius at Adrianople and Chrysopolis. The wars were struggles for imperial power, but they created the first Christian emperor and the first Christian theology of victory in battle.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/story:
By 306 the system of four co-emperors created by Diocletian had collapsed into rivalry. Constantine was proclaimed emperor by his father's troops at York; Maxentius, son of the retired emperor Maximian, seized Rome. At the same time the Great Persecution of Christians, begun in 303, was ending unevenly: Galerius issued an edict of toleration in 311, but persecution continued for a while in the East under Maximinus Daia. Christians thus had strong reasons to watch the emperors' contest closely.

In spring 312 Constantine crossed the Alps from Gaul with a relatively small army, perhaps forty thousand men, took Segusio (Susa), defeated Maxentius' heavy cavalry near Turin, captured Milan, and won a hard battle at Verona, where Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus was killed. He then marched on Rome. Maxentius, who had prepared the city for a siege, unexpectedly came out to fight and drew up his army with the Tiber at its back near the Milvian Bridge.

The religious tradition about the battle comes from two Christian authors who knew Constantine. Lactantius, writing about 314–315, says Constantine was told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields, a Chi-Rho or staurogram. Eusebius, in his Life of Constantine written after the emperor's death in 337, reports the emperor's own sworn account of a cross of light seen in the sky with the words 'by this conquer' (in Greek, touto nika; in Latin tradition, in hoc signo vinces), followed by a dream in which Christ told him to make a standard of the sign, the labarum. On 28 October 312 Maxentius' army broke; the retreat across a temporary bridge of boats collapsed and Maxentius drowned in the Tiber. Constantine entered Rome, had Maxentius' head paraded on a spear, and dissolved the praetorian guard.

Early in 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan and agreed the policy of religious freedom and restitution of Christian property usually called the Edict of Milan. Licinius then defeated Maximinus Daia, who had resumed persecution, near Adrianople; Lactantius claims Licinius' soldiers recited a prayer to the 'Supreme God' given by an angel. The two victors soon fell out. A first war in 316–317 brought battles at Cibalae and Mardia and gave Constantine most of the Balkans. Over the following years Licinius, suspecting Christians of loyalty to his rival, expelled them from his household and army, restricted church synods and was accused of further harassment.

In 324 Constantine attacked again, now presenting himself as protector of Christians in the East. He defeated Licinius at Adrianople on 3 July; his son Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont; and on 18 September Constantine won the decisive battle of Chrysopolis on the Asian shore of the Bosporus. Eusebius describes the labarum carried before the army, a tent of prayer in the camp and priests accompanying the troops. Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia after his wife Constantia, Constantine's sister, pleaded for his life; he was promised safety but was executed at Thessalonica in 325, as was his young son a little later.

As sole emperor Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea in 325 and founded Constantinople, dedicated in 330, on the site of the old Byzantium near the scene of his final victory. Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History and Life of Constantine framed the whole sequence as God's deliverance of his church through a chosen emperor, a reading that shaped Christian political thought for more than a thousand years and made the cross a military emblem.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/nameOfGod: Constantine's soldiers fought under the Chi-Rho painted on their shields (Lactantius) and behind the labarum, a jewelled standard bearing the Chi-Rho, which Eusebius says had power to give victory and was guarded by a special detachment. The vision's message, 'by this conquer' (in hoc signo vinces), became the classic formula of the cross as a sign of victory. Eusebius portrayed Licinius as a new Pharaoh and Constantine as a new Moses, and described prayers in a portable tabernacle before battle. The triumphal Arch of Constantine (315) diplomatically credits victory to 'the inspiration of the divinity' (instinctu divinitatis) without naming Christ.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/religiousCauses: Constantine's belief, from 312, that the God of the Christians had granted him victory and would continue to do so if properly honoured.
The recent Great Persecution (303–311/313) gave Christians, and Constantine's propaganda, an interest in which emperors would protect or persecute the church.
Licinius' later restrictions on Christians allowed Constantine to frame the war of 324 as the liberation of eastern Christians from a persecutor.
Eusebius' providential theology, in which the emperor is God's agent on earth, gave the wars a sacred meaning after the event.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/otherCauses/0: The breakdown of the Tetrarchy after Diocletian's abdication in 305 left several men with armies and claims to the purple.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/otherCauses/1: Constantine's personal ambition and dynastic claim as son of Constantius I, and his wish to unite the empire under one ruler and his sons.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/otherCauses/2: Control of Rome, Italy and the wealthy eastern provinces, with their tax revenues and armies.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/otherCauses/3: Mutual suspicion and broken agreements between Constantine and Licinius after 313, including disputes over Caesars appointed for their sons.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/triggers/0: Maxentius' declaration of war on Constantine, ostensibly to avenge his father Maximian, gave Constantine the occasion to invade Italy in 312.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/triggers/1: The elevation of Bassianus and a disputed plot in 316 led to the first war between Constantine and Licinius.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/triggers/2: Constantine's pursuit of Sarmatian and Gothic raiders into Licinius' territory in 323 provoked the final war of 324.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/0/text: Diocletian launches the Great Persecution of Christians.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/1/text: Constantine proclaimed emperor at York; Maxentius seizes Rome.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/2/text: Galerius' edict of toleration ends persecution in much of the empire.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/3/text: Constantine invades Italy, wins at Turin and Verona, and defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/4/text: Constantine and Licinius agree the 'Edict of Milan'; Licinius defeats Maximinus Daia.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/5/text: The Arch of Constantine is dedicated in Rome, crediting victory to the 'divinity'.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/6/text: First war between Constantine and Licinius: battles of Cibalae and Mardia (316–317).
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/7/text: Licinius begins to purge Christians from his court and army and restrict church synods.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/8/text: Constantine defeats Licinius at Adrianople (July), at sea in the Hellespont, and at Chrysopolis (18 September).
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/9/text: Licinius executed at Thessalonica; Constantine summons the Council of Nicaea.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/timeline/10/tex: Constantinople dedicated near the site of the final victory.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/0/foc: Invaded Italy in 312, fought under the Chi-Rho at the Milvian Bridge, and defeated Licinius in 316–317 and 324.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/0/out: Sole emperor from 324; patron of the church, convener of Nicaea, baptised on his deathbed in 337 and venerated as a saint in the East.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/1/foc: Held Rome against Constantine; came out to fight at the Milvian Bridge.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/1/out: Drowned in the Tiber during the rout; his memory was condemned and he was later depicted as a tyrant.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/2/foc: Ally of Constantine in 313, then his rival in two wars; later restricted Christians in his domains.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/2/out: Defeated at Chrysopolis, surrendered at Nicomedia and executed in 325 despite a promise of safety.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/3/foc: Recorded Constantine's account of the vision and interpreted the wars as God's deliverance of the church.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/3/out: His Ecclesiastical History and Life of Constantine founded the Christian imperial ideal of the 'Christian emperor'.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/4/rol: Christian rhetorician and tutor to Constantine's son Crispus
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/4/foc: Earliest source for the dream and the heavenly sign on the shields in On the Deaths of the Persecutors.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/4/out: His work is the main near-contemporary Christian narrative of the persecutions and civil wars.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/5/foc: Destroyed Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont in 324.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/keyPeople/5/out: Executed on his father's orders in 326 for reasons never explained.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/casualties/note: No credible figures survive for losses at Turin, Verona, the Milvian Bridge, Cibalae, Adrianople or Chrysopolis; ancient numbers for army sizes (for example Zosimus' claim of very large forces at Chrysopolis) are generally regarded as exaggerated, so no estimate range is given.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effects/0: Constantine became master of the West in 312 and of the whole empire in 324, ending the Tetrarchy.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effects/1: The church gained legal security, restored property and growing imperial patronage after 313.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effects/2: A new capital, Constantinople, was founded near the site of the final victory.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effects/3: The cross and Chi-Rho became imperial and military emblems, carried on standards for centuries.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effects/4: Emperors began to intervene directly in church disputes, starting with the Donatist controversy and Nicaea.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/effectsOnChurch: Christianity moved from a persecuted minority to an imperially favoured religion within a decade.
Eusebius' theology of the Christian emperor as God's vice-regent shaped Byzantine and later Western political theology.
The earlier strong Christian reluctance about military service weakened; the Council of Arles (314) penalised soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.
The association of the cross with military victory laid foundations for later ideas of holy war, though not yet for crusade.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/legacy: The Milvian Bridge became one of the hinges of Christian history: the beginning of 'Constantinian' Christianity, praised by Eusebius and much of the later church as providential and criticised by Anabaptists, many modern theologians and historians of Christian pacifism as the moment the church accepted the sword. The phrase 'in this sign conquer' was later used by crusaders, monarchies and military orders. Historians continue to debate what Constantine saw, perhaps a solar halo phenomenon, and how far his conversion shaped his policies.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/dissenters/0/te: In his Divine Institutes (c. 303–311), written before he became a court writer, Lactantius taught that a just man may not serve as a soldier and that killing a human being is always wrong, a view that sat uneasily with his later celebration of Constantine's victories.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/dissenters/1/te: A generation later, in 356, Martin, then serving in the army of Constantine's son Constantius II under the Caesar Julian, reportedly refused a donative before battle saying 'I am a soldier of Christ; it is not lawful for me to fight' (Sulpicius Severus, Life of Martin), showing that the older Christian reluctance about war survived within the Christian empire.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/dissenters/2/te: Pre-Constantinian writers such as Tertullian and Origen had argued that Christians should not shed blood in war; their views were remembered, though increasingly marginal, after 312.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/theatres/3/name: Battle of the Milvian Bridge (Saxa Rubra)
conflicts/milvian-bridge/campaigns/0/peo: Constantine and his Gallic and Rhine army
conflicts/milvian-bridge/campaigns/0/tex: Crossing the Alps by the Mont Cenis route, Constantine took Susa, beat Maxentius' cavalry at Turin, was welcomed at Milan, broke the northern army at Verona and marched down the Via Flaminia to the Tiber, where Maxentius was defeated and drowned on 28 October.
conflicts/milvian-bridge/campaigns/1/peo: Constantine, with Crispus commanding the fleet
conflicts/milvian-bridge/campaigns/1/tex: From his base at Thessalonica Constantine advanced into Thrace, won at Adrianople on 3 July, besieged Byzantium while Crispus cleared the Hellespont, crossed to Asia and won the decisive battle of Chrysopolis on 18 September; Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia.
